title: How I use AI in game dev while retaining full creative control
author: PoorSquirrrel
selftext:
After reading one too many "here's the game I made with one prompt" postings, I thought I'd share what I do instead, which is quite different from that.

Context: I have been developing games for a few decades now, so AI is the new part, not game dev. That might explain some.

The screenshot shows what my project looks like right now. Underwhelming, right? Well here's the kicker: It's fully playable. I'm using AI to do something that I've never done before because it's too much effort for a solo dev who thrives on "exploration writing" (I also write, exploration writing is basically when you as the author discover the story as you write it instead of planning out everything in advance).

**Greyboxing** \- this is what you see in the screenshot. It's a battle-tested game dev principle. Build the whole game with zero art first to test out the core mechanics. Only when you've got those down do you go and add graphics, sounds, effects, etc. etc.



https://i.redd.it/n1wnkdqg6yyh1.png

My experience: AI is utterly **amazing** at greyboxing. It makes it so much easier for the AI to understand what it is working with if everything is simple shapes and the vision part of Claude Code (which is what I'm using) can instantly understand what everything is. Close to zero misunderstandings.

This feeds into my second principle:

**Iterative feature sessions** \- in every session, I focus on one and only one thing. And I'll tell Claude at the beginning what it is. "In this session, we will build the UI" or "In this session, we optimize the layout". Then I work in many, many iterations with small prompts instead of a giant wall of text. This way I can do micro-management and correct any mistakes before they balloon out into an entire system. I typically run a few dozen iterations on every feature before I'm satisfied. Then I clear the context and start the next thing.

**Let AI write the design doc** \- I've instructed Claude to create and continuously update the design documentation. This gives me another layer to check and correct. And it stores design decisions in a context-size-friendly way. I've always been too lazy to write extensive docs, and now Claude just keeps a record of the decisions I make during the iterative process.

**Tests,** oh yeah! - I've always been way too lazy to write tests. So I rarely did. They also need to be updated - ugh. But telling Claude to generate tests for everything it creates and to run them after every major change is easy. And it gives me yet another layer to check its work, and it's free regression testing - no fear that feature B today trashes feature A from yesterday. What's not to love?



And finally: I build and use **skills** extensively - I've spent an entire session just feeding it reference material and discussing what "fun" is and which elements and challenges I want to use in this game. Now I have a skill that contains all that knowledge and decisions and I can re-use it for the next project. There's half a dozen other skills in this project for other specific parts of the work.

  
So yeah, that's an insight of how I personally use AI. There's still a lot of manual work that I add, both in the Unity (my engine) editor and in code, etc. - for me the AI is a junior coder that I can give tasks and a rubber ducky to discuss ideas with. It's been a great companion so far to quickly test out ideas or different versions of systems. All the creative decisions are still made by me, and I'm not AI-generating art (except the greyboxes that'll eventually get replaced).

Just thought I'd give a different perspective on how AI can be used in game development without giving away creative control.

comments.author: Chocoweb88
comments.body: Thanks for the sharing! Very insightful for my future project moving forward.

comments.author: Kanalbanan
comments.body: Yes totally agree, I’ve been using greyboxing too and just like in game development without ai it helps a lot.

comments.author: PsychologicalArt2537
comments.body:
Agreeing with all points. Plus 
1. create yourself a skill to save learnings in a session. Your AI agent can mistakes and can learn not to make mistakes in future. Instruct claude to call this skill before any commit.
2. For godot, keep a downloaded copy of source code. I ran into engine level bugs or optimisation issues few times. Having a copy of the source code helps.
3. Create all features in work tree and while landing into main, run the full test suite.

replies.author: PoorSquirrrel
replies.body: Totally, using recap or another similar skill to save learnings in memory is essential.

comments.author: Puffelpuff
comments.body:
I have a different approach. 

I greybox first and add placeholder assets generated by codex. each chat has its own context and while i retain guides and worflows in a bible folder. each time i get to work on something, i go to the specific chat assigned to as task. Demo worker, code worker, art worker, 3d worker, coordinator, figma worker are usually the big ones. Once an asset is finished its added to the bible with its full workflow and i move on to the next one. I found wiping the chats context too often or opening a new chat for coding tasks was eating a fuck ton of tokens. Old large chats compact context anyway and refer to the bible for more while building and refining skills. I can´t stress enough how important having context bibles is. Game mechanics each getting their own doc, all alignments neatly folded into context based documents and more importantly having a code reference base for the AI to check where it can find specific mechanics so it does not have to search the whole code. 

for how i approach design docs, i write them myself, have them reformted by the AI while checking for open question, answer those and get to a point where i as the designer am satisfied with the result. this can take days, even weeks are not unusual. the human touch is what lets the tool shine. 

Lastly, claude is amazing for art if you can point it in the right direction with codex providing the actual assets itself with tripo for 3d and texture generation. I found meshy way to messy is inconsistent.

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: the greybox first approach makes a lot of sense. one thing i would add is writing the expected player result before asking AI for tests. otherwise it can make tests that only confirm what its own code already does, including the wrong behavior.

comments.author: Stalins_Ghost
comments.body: You have to let a bit go. If you control a human team you do not have 100% control of the outcome either. You just need to be disciplined with AI and do not do woek when you're tired and impatient it is when thinga start slipping.

comments.author: Epyx911
comments.body: Did this as well, along with a full design doc and ruleset (crpg). Best AI use is iterative.

comments.author: Charming-Network-456
comments.body: I agree wholeheartedly. And I'll bet that you don't have issues with token usage. I work similarly and I've found it's not easy to "burn" through my tokens in any given 5 hour window. I see that as a symptom of asking an AI to do something the human themselves have no idea how to specify.

replies.author: PoorSquirrrel
replies.body: Rarely. I have managed to hit my weekly quota, but that was during a week where I also used Claude for other token-intensive tasks.
